I am a 61-year-old farmer from Quzhou County, and I have been working my family’s land for over forty years. Around here, the soil is good flat alluvial soil, and we have reliable well irrigation, so the only sensible way to use the land is the double-cropping system that everyone in the village follows: winter wheat followed by summer maize. I have 6 mu in total. Last October I sowed improved wheat varieties—nothing fancy, just the reliable semi-dwarf varieties recommended by the agricultural station in town. Now that spring is starting and the wheat is greening up, my focus is on managing that crop through to the June harvest, then immediately switching to maize. I do not experiment with new crops like vegetables or soybeans because the market is uncertain and my family depends on the stable grain subsidy and the familiar buyers who come to the village. For wheat, I will apply fertilizer in three splits, irrigate three times, and spray twice for weeds and insects. For maize, I will plant hybrid seed directly into the wheat stubble with minimal tillage right after harvest, irrigate once or twice depending on the rains, and keep chemicals to a minimum to control costs.
